content: I'm getting tired of off-by-one indexing with TFAE (as a reminder, the propositions are numbered from 1 to n in the proof, but then from 0 to n-1 in TFAE.out). I think numbering starting from zero is the most sensible, would everyone be okay with this change?
What about switching to 1-indexing in TFAE.out? :eyes: An argument for this would be that the list should be an implementation detail, and 1, 2, 3… are closer to ordinary mathematical practice
(I do also think it would be nice eventually to have better notation for TFAE that showed the numbers, and it would be a bit odd for that to start at 0)
Strong agreement with making things consistent. Weak agreement with 1-based numbering.
I think 1-based is confusing given that it's just backed by a list that is 0-indexed (at least as far as I recall)
I agree with Ruben, I would just use 0-based indexing like we do for almost everything.
(Also, this is not a strong argument, but switching to 0-based indexing is a much lighter change, because one only has to changes the TFAE proofs, as opposed to their use places)

I feel like there is a big difference between the 0-based indexing in programming (where indices are arithmetic objects) and the 1-based enumeration in natural language. TFAE feels like it falls cleanly in the latter.
Can someone point out anything else in Lean that is 1-indexed (except maybe docs#PNat)?

• nth_rw is 1-indexed
  • to_dual (reorder := 1 2 3) is 1-indexed
  • conv => enter [4] is 1-indexed (and 0 has the special meaning of entering into the head function).

Lie/Killing.lean
It's probably not what you meant by "in Lean", but that's kinda the point
nth_grw is 1-indexed, like nth_rw
Minor, but when refine or similar creates goals, they are 1-indexed (e.g. refine_1)
Generally I feel tactic and elab interfaces lean towards 1-indexing, which is one reason I think 1-indexing fits here.

But the more important reason for 1-indexing, I think, is that we do want to match mathematical practice where reasonable, making lean/mathlib more familiar to mathematicians. I think we often see in natural language

TFAE:
1. ...
2. ...
...

but quite rarely

TFAE:
0. ...
1. ...
...

Also, I believe that since we are not relying on any mathematical properties of the natural numbers (they are effectively just source labels), we ought to choose the right interface on the basis of ergonomics/readability and then engineer the API/implementation to match, rather than choosing the implementation (Lists) and then designing the interface around it :) I agree that our API currently does not present a single, coherent interface (and it should)!

A while ago I suggested making the to_dual (reorder := ...) syntax be 0-indexed, but I was then convinced that this was not a good idea.

My understanding now of the convention is that we prefer 0-indexing when the index is an actual expression of type Nat, and we prefer 1-indexing when the index is a number literal that is part of some special user facing syntax.

So, maybe the solution is to create some special user facing syntax (i.e. a term elaborator) to get information out of a TFAE statement.

(There has in the past been discussion about the possibility of being able to name certain TFAE components (e.g. not just 1 but MyProp), so the elab approach might open up other possibilities as well)
Do we actually care about the numbers in TFAE.out? My impression was that TFAE.out was only ever used to help set up a better-named API, and that we presumably care more about tfae_have
Maybe the fact they already differ is an argument for entirely replacing the numbers in the proof with names

I've opened #42663 to move Mathlib to a 1-indexed TFAE out.
I should ask: does anyone have any strong opposition to 1-indexing after this discussion?

Note: I had Claude write an awk script to do the migration; not sure if this belongs in scripts/ so that downstream users can refactor too.

#! /usr/bin/env bash

 : <<'BASH_MODULE_DOC'

`TFAE.out` used to take 0-indexed indices and now takes 1-indexed ones, matching the numbering
used by the `tfae` tactics. Mathlib's own call sites have already been migrated; this script is
kept for downstream projects, which have to migrate theirs. In every `.lean` file below the given
directories, an application of `.out` to two decimal literals has both literals incremented.

  scripts/bump_tfae_out.sh DIR [DIR ...]

The whitespace separating `.out` from its arguments is arbitrary (a call may span a line break)
and is preserved, as is whatever follows the second literal.

Requiring *two* literals is what makes the rewrite safe: the other `.out` projections in the
library (`Fact.out`, `Quotient.out`, `OrdConnected.out`, ...) are never applied to two adjacent
numerals. `TFAE.out'`, the deprecated 0-indexed version, is safe for the same reason and because
`out` must be followed by whitespace to match at all.

A call site of the form `.out <numeral> <non-numeral>` is therefore left alone. Such sites are
not `TFAE.out` calls in mathlib itself, but to list them in your own project and check by hand:

  grep -rn --include='*.lean' -E '[.]out[[:space:]]+[0-9]+[^0-9[:space:]]' DIR

Each rewritten file is reported on stderr as `path: <number of call sites>`.

BASH_MODULE_DOC

set -euo pipefail

if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "usage: $0 DIR [DIR ...]" >&2
  exit 1
fi

prog='
# Buffer the file, since a call site may span a line break.
{ buf = buf $0 "\n" }

END {
  while (match(buf, /\.out[ \t\r\n]+[0-9]+[ \t\r\n]+[0-9]+/)) {
    out = out substr(buf, 1, RSTART - 1)         # everything before the call site
    args = substr(buf, RSTART + 4, RLENGTH - 4)  # the whitespace and literals after ".out"
    buf = substr(buf, RSTART + RLENGTH)

    match(args, /[0-9]+/)                        # first literal, with the whitespace before it
    ws1 = substr(args, 1, RSTART - 1)
    i = substr(args, RSTART, RLENGTH) + 0
    args = substr(args, RSTART + RLENGTH)

    match(args, /[0-9]+/)                        # second literal, likewise
    ws2 = substr(args, 1, RSTART - 1)
    j = substr(args, RSTART, RLENGTH) + 0

    out = out sprintf(".out%s%d%s%d", ws1, i + 1, ws2, j + 1)
    n++
  }
  printf "%s", out buf
  if (n) printf "%s: %d\n", FILENAME, n > "/dev/stderr"
}'

# `.lake` is skipped so that vendored copies of mathlib are left alone.
find "$@" -name '*.lean' -not -path '*/.lake/*' -print |
while IFS= read -r f; do
  awk "$prog" "$f" > "$f.bump"
  if cmp -s "$f" "$f.bump"; then rm "$f.bump"; else mv "$f.bump" "$f"; fi
done

Or just t[1 ↔ 2]? That would be easier to implement; but either way, both are mainly going to be some macro rules + a term elaborator:

Prototype

import Mathlib

syntax "tfae_extract% " term:max term:max term:max &"imp"? : term

macro_rules
  | `($proof[$l ↔ $r]) => `(tfae_extract% $proof $l $r)
  | `($proof[$l →%$tk $r]) => `(tfae_extract% $proof $l $r imp%$tk)

open Lean Meta Elab Term Qq

elab_rules : term
  | `(tfae_extract% $proof $l $r $[imp%$impTk]?) => do
    let exTy? : Option Expr := ‹_›
    let state ← saveState
    let proofExpr ← elabTerm proof none
    unless ← isProof proofExpr do
      -- who knows, maybe someone does crazy stuff like this
      state.restore
      let inner ← if impTk.isSome then `($l → $r) else `($l ↔ $r)
      return ← elabTerm (← `(getElem $proof $inner (by get_elem_tactic))) exTy?
    let props : Q(List Prop) ← mkFreshExprMVarQ q(List Prop)
    let proofExpr : Q(List.TFAE $props) ← Term.ensureHasType q(List.TFAE $props) proofExpr
    let mut propArray : Array Q(Prop) := #[]
    let mut propIter := props
    repeat
      propIter ← whnf propIter
      if propIter.isAppOfArity ``List.cons 3 then
        propArray := propArray.push propIter.appFn!.appArg!
        propIter := propIter.appArg!
      else if propIter.isAppOfArity ``List.nil 1 then
        break
      else
        throwError "Error: Input to {.ofConstName ``List.TFAE} is not a list literal:{indentExpr props}"
    let rec locate (t : Term) : TermElabM Nat := do
      if let some n := t.raw.isNatLit? then
        if n = 0 then
          throwErrorAt t "Invalid index 0, indices in TFAE count from 1"
        if propArray.size < n then
          throwErrorAt t "Invalid index {n}, the TFAE only includes {propArray.size} propositions"
        return n - 1
      let pattern ← elabTermEnsuringTypeQ t q(Prop)
      let mctx ← getMCtx
      for h : i in *...propArray.size do
        if ← withReducible <| isDefEq propArray[i] pattern then
          return i
        setMCtx mctx
      throwErrorAt t "Couldn't find pattern{indentExpr pattern}"
    let lidx : Nat ← locate l
    let ridx : Nat ← locate r
    have lprop := propArray[lidx]!
    have rprop := propArray[ridx]!
    have hl : Q($props[$lidx]? = some $lprop) := show Q(some $lprop = some $lprop) from q(rfl)
    have hr : Q($props[$ridx]? = some $rprop) := show Q(some $rprop = some $rprop) from q(rfl)
    have iff : Q($lprop ↔ $rprop) := q($proofExpr $lprop (List.mem_of_getElem? $hl) $rprop (List.mem_of_getElem? $hr))
    if impTk.isSome then
      return q(Iff.mp $iff)
    else
      return iff

so we'd have something like

structure A : Prop
structure B : Prop
structure C : Prop

theorem test : List.TFAE [A, B, C] := by
  tfae_have 1 → 2 := fun _ => ⟨⟩
  tfae_have 2 → 3 := fun _ => ⟨⟩
  tfae_have 3 → 1 := fun _ => ⟨⟩
  tfae_finish

example : True := by
  have h₁ := test[1 ↔ 2]
  have h₂ := test[A ↔ C]
  have h₃ := test[C ↔ B]
  have h₄ := test[C → B]
  have h₅ := test[C → 1]
  have h₆ := test[2 → C]

We could also have

theorem List.TFAE.infer (h : List.TFAE l) : List.TFAE l := h

then if we wanted the benefits of dot notation :-)

And for whoever would ever want it,

can also keep working

Maybe it’s fine! I’m getting used to it the more I stare at it. :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes: And I think doing the same thing but for : (i.e. t : 1 ↔︎ 2, etc., so it looked like a coercion) would probably be unreasonable?
Maybe have h : P <-> Q := by tfae [my_tfae_lemma] is more in Mathlib style, where a tactic helps create a term, instead of more bespoke term syntax?

(My other thought is that I still would like to implement the tactic/environment extension infer I have, say 3/4 planned, and so it might be nice to plan for a unified interface centered around the infer keyword. But we shouldn’t let that stand in the way of better notation.)
(Oh, I suppose infer t : 1 ↔︎ 2 is another slightly more concise option in the infer vein. I might be reinventing ideas from old threads at this point. :laughing:)
